newsitem.title: CANADA: ATHLETICS-BAILEY, JOHNSON SET FOR MILLION DOLLAR DUEL.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BAILEY, JOHNSON SET FOR MILLION DOLLAR DUEL.

text.p: It wasn't Ali versus Frazier, but sprinters Donovan Bailey and Michael Johnson continued their verbal jousting ahead of Sunday's million-dollar duel for the title of world's fastest man.
Less than 48 hours before the so-called One to One Challenge of Champions, both Olympic gold medallists said they were confident of victory in the race over the compromise distance of 150 meters.
"I am naturally faster," Bailey, the 100-meter gold medal winner in Atlanta last summer, said during a frenzied press conference in Toronto Friday.
Johnson, Olympic champion in the 200 and 400 meters, said he was willing to put both athletes' $500,000 appearance fees as well as the prize money up for grabs in a winner-take-all bet.
"I would put the whole $2 million on the line because I feel that confident. I felt confident before and I remain confident now," Johnson, 30, said.
Bailey declined to take the challenge, saying that running was his job now. He also denied reports that he was suffering from a knee injury.
"I'm bigger, stronger, heavier and faster" (than a year ago), the 30-year-old Jamaican-born Canadian said.
As workers laid down the 150-meter track in Toronto's SkyDome Stadium, race organisers said 38,000 tickets had been sold so far.
About 400 media from around the world are in Toronto for the race, which will be broadcast to a potential audience of 300 million.

"Yes, the event is happening. The atheletes are in town," said Giselle Briden, president of Magellan Entertainment Group Inc. She denied media reports that the promoter was running out of cash and confirmed the athletes have been paid.
Some athletes in other events have bailed out due to injury or other reasons, including star pole vaulter Sergei Bubka.
Head-to-head events scheduled for Sunday include the pole vault, long jump, high jump, culminating in the Bailey/Johnson showdown.
Sunday's clash was born at the Atlanta Games where Bailey ran the 100 meters in a world-record 9.84 seconds. The 100-meter winner has been considered the world's fastest human.
But Johnson set off the debate when he ran the 200 meters in 19.32 seconds, a world record.
Asked if the race will end the debate over who is the fastest once and for all, Bailey said: "That was settled in Atlanta."
Of Johnson's claim that he is the quickest, Bailey said: "The media has drummed it into his head, and he feels like this is something he needs."
Johnson said Bailey has never given him the respect he deserved. "I've always had respect for him. He has downplayed some of my accomplishments and not given me the respect that I am due," he said.
The race has stirred patriotic passions among Canadians who felt slighted when the American media branded Johnson the world's fleetest human.
Canadian newspapers published special sections on the race, including glossy photos of Bailey wrapped in a Canadian flag after his Olympic victory.
The Canadian broadcaster has run ads encouraging viewers to tune in because "this is your chance to gloat Canada."
Johnson acknowledged some are portraying the race as Canada versus the United States. But he does not share the feeling.

"I'm not looking at it as an American versus Canadian thing. I don't think most Americans look at that way. The Canadians have had a great time looking at it as a Canadian versus America thing and that's fine if it makes them feel good," he said.
Asked if he was running for Canadian pride, Bailey, who trains in Texas, demurred, saying: "It's really good to be home. There's a lot of electricity in the air and it's good to be here."
